Eschatological Kingdom
es-kat-oh-LAH-jih-kul KING-dum
noun phrase
From Greek eschatos (last, final, uttermost) + logos (word, discourse) + Old English cyningdom (kingdom, dominion of a king). The “eschatological kingdom” distinguishes the final, consummated form of God’s reign from the present inaugurated kingdom: not merely that God now rules, but that His rule will be visibly and universally manifested in the age to come when Christ delivers all things to the Father.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The eschatological kingdom is the fully consummated form of God’s reign—the age to come in which Christ’s present lordship is completed in universal, visible, bodily glory. Scripture moves from the inauguration of the kingdom (in Christ’s first coming, death, and resurrection) toward its final consummation at His return. Daniel’s vision is foundational: the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, which shall crush all opposing kingdoms and stand forever (Dan. 2:44). At the seventh trumpet of Revelation the proclamation comes: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ—and He will reign forever and ever” (Rev. 11:15). Paul’s eschatological sequence in 1 Corinthians 15 describes the consummation: Christ reigns until He has put all enemies under His feet, the last enemy being death; then He delivers the kingdom to the Father (1 Cor. 15:24–28). This is not the end of Christ’s reign but its glorified completion: the Son’s mediatorial kingdom, prosecuted through history, handed up in triumph to the Father who is all in all. Peter promises that an entrance into “the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Pet. 1:11) is richly supplied to those who grow in grace. The eschatological kingdom is thus the goal of redemptive history, the inheritance of the saints, the final state of the cosmos renewed, and the end toward which all of creation groans (Rom. 8:19–22). Reformed eschatology reads this as the already-not-yet tension: the kingdom is here (in the church, in the Spirit’s work, in Christ’s risen lordship) and still coming (in bodily resurrection, final judgment, and new creation).

Webster 1828 Definition

Eschatology: the department of theology treating of the last things; the doctrine of death, resurrection, judgment, and the final state of man and the world; the consummation of God’s kingdom.

expand to see more

ES-CHA-TOL'O-GY, noun. (Theology) The doctrine of the last things; that part of systematic theology treating of death, the resurrection of the body, the last judgment, and the final state of the righteous and the wicked.

2. (Kingdom of God) The final and consummated form of God's reign—that ultimate state toward which the present age moves and in which Christ's lordship is fully manifested in glory without remainder.

KING'DOM OF GOD. (Consummated) The eternal kingdom established by God which shall never be destroyed (Dan. 2:44); the state of perfect blessedness and righteous order in which God reigns visibly over all creation.

4. Distinguished from the ‘inaugurated kingdom’—the present age in which Christ's kingdom is real but veiled; the eschatological kingdom removes the veil and is the direct, unmediated reign of God and the Lamb.

Webster's classical eschatological framework reflects the historic Christian consensus across Reformed, Lutheran, and Catholic traditions that history has a terminus and a goal: the full realization of God's sovereign reign.

Key Scripture

Revelation 11:15 — "And the seventh angel sounded — and there were loud voices in heaven, saying: 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ — and He will reign forever and ever.'"

1 Corinthians 15:24 — "Then comes the end — when He hands over the kingdom to the God and Father, when He has abolished all rule and all authority and power."

2 Peter 1:11 — "for in this way, the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you."

Daniel 2:44 — "And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever."

Modern Corruption

Dispensational premillennialism divides the eschatological kingdom into a Jewish earthly millennial phase and a later eternal phase, introducing a distinction the New Testament does not support; liberal theology de-eschatologizes the kingdom entirely into a present social-ethical project.

expand to see more

Classic dispensationalism (Darby, Scofield, Chafer) bifurcates the kingdom into two programs: a present “church age” parenthesis with no kingdom; a future Jewish earthly millennial kingdom in which the Old Testament promises to national Israel are fulfilled in Jerusalem; and then—finally—an eternal state. This scheme requires reading the New Testament as a theological parenthesis in God’s Jewish national plan, produces a theology with two peoples of God under two covenants, and drives a hermeneutic in which the Old Testament prophetic promises are interpreted literally-nationally rather than Christologically and ecclesiologically. The New Testament itself collapses this: the church is the Israel of God (Gal. 6:16), the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and in His seed (Gal. 3:16, 26–29), and the kingdom Christ announces is not a deferred national restoration but a present-and-coming cosmic reign.

On the left, liberal theology in the tradition of Albrecht Ritschl and Adolph Harnack evacuated the kingdom of its eschatological content, reading it as the progressive realization of God’s fatherhood and human brotherhood through social reform—what the Social Gospel movement called building the kingdom on earth. Albert Schweitzer’s critique exposed this as projecting modern liberal ethics onto Jesus; Karl Barth’s recovery of eschatological seriousness helped, but the impulse persists in liberation theology and progressive evangelicalism, which collapse the future kingdom into present political activism. The Reformed answer is the already-not-yet: the kingdom is present in power and yet awaiting its consummation—neither pure futurity nor pure present social program, but the progressive victorious advance of Christ’s reign through history toward a final, glorious terminus.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eschatos (last) and basileia (kingdom) together name the final form of the reign that was inaugurated in Christ’s resurrection and will be consummated in His return.

expand to see more

Greek eschatos — last, final, uttermost; the root of “eschatology”—the study of the last things and the final state toward which all history moves

Greek basileia — kingdom, reign, royal rule; the New Testament's standard term for God's sovereign reign—both present (Matt. 12:28) and coming (Matt. 6:10)

Hebrew malkuth — kingdom, dominion, reign; Daniel's term for the eternal kingdom that the God of heaven will establish (Dan. 2:44; 4:3)

Greek telos — end, goal, consummation; 1 Cor. 15:24's term for the moment Christ delivers the kingdom to the Father—the eschatological terminus of redemptive history

Greek parousia — presence, arrival, coming; the technical NT term for Christ's return, at which the eschatological kingdom arrives in its final consummated form

Usage

"The already-not-yet framework (inaugurated eschatology, associated especially with Geerhardus Vos and George Ladd) is the Reformed consensus: the kingdom is genuinely present in Christ's resurrection, His lordship, and the Spirit's work, but it is not yet fully manifested—the consummation awaits His bodily return."

"The eschatological kingdom relativizes all present political kingdoms: they are provisional, transient, and accountable to the coming Kingdom of Christ—which means Christians engage politics with both hope and detachment, knowing the final outcome is not in human hands."

"The new creation is the spatial/material dimension of the eschatological kingdom: the consummated kingdom does not merely inhabit a reconstituted spiritual realm but fills a renewed cosmos—‘the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea’ (Isa. 11:9)."
